items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I met her, fell in love immediately, and the two of us were like 12 hours a day... And she helped me put on the Great Night in Harlem.

ctx.x: Didn’t another one of your angels give you the go-ahead for that?

That’s what I wanted to get into. That whole thing came about when I had this idea to do a concert at the Apollo. My Board looked at me like, “Little girl, you’re not a concert producer; we’re not concert producers—and how much is the Apollo?” It was $15,000 to rent at the time. That’s what they said. This was before they got bigger, their recent incarnation. So I called up one of our new board members, who... I had asked them, “Who do we know who has any money?” and they gave me the name of this guy, Jarrett…

We didn’t know what we were doing. I want to say at this point, and introduce the next great person who came into our midst. Not just Jarrett Lilien, who ended up saving the day and then becoming our president, who has been my partner in this for years. But Lauren Roberts, who... When they handed me the keys to this place with the $7,000 in the bank, I was the only employee—that was going to be that. I needed someone. I couldn’t do this alone. We were getting to the point where we were starting to see now, from…

items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026
items.q: So I contacted a friend of mine... he sent one of his students who turned out to be the most brilliant young woman... Lauren Roberts. And the two of us in nine weeks put this together.

ctx.x: Yeah, right. And Milt Hinton and these fellas who played on these rock & roll records and all that, the story is completely fascinating to me.

It’s beyond. And we know all the earlier racism, everyone knows the clubs, the labels, the record companies, we know so many things that went down back then. There was one story that really stands out in my early moments, and I’ll segue into the Great Night in Harlem and answer your question, but there was a legend who – I think it was Ron Carter who came to me and said, “I ran into someone at the airport and he didn’t have a seeing eye cane but he was blind as a bat, he really couldn’t see where he was going.”…

coming back and I introduced him, I asked him to do a gig with this young musician and they got tight. And before we knew it young musicians were asking him to sit in at clubs. So he would guest star. So he was making money. They were getting paid more because they had the famous name and they were becoming like family. So this became a little thing that started happening with some of the elders. So many beautiful things. So okay, Great Night in Harlem. I really didn’t know anything about jazz. In fact I could…
